AN IMPORTANT QUESTION.

Sir,—Will you very kindly allow me, through the medium of your paper, to try and get an answer to an important question, which has been asked me over and over again by those brave men (chiefly married men with wives and families) who have joined our Territorial Force in defence of our King and country? MA- is it that there are still so many young men in Warrington, with no one depending upon them, walking aimlessly about, curtailing none of their pleasures, denying themselves of noth- ing, appearing as thongh nothing serious had happened? I should be glad if these young men, to whom my comrades refer, would answer this question bi joining, them as soon as possible. W3l. BRACECAMP, Chaplain 4th Battalion P.W.V. (South Lancashire Regiment). St. Paul's Vicarage; Warrington, August 13th, 1914.
NO PARTY POLITICS. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space to in- form the members of the Progressive Labour

-LaTiu.e--;:nctiothers who attend the weekly meet- ings at Bridge Foot that owing to the war the meetings will be postponed until further notice? Whatever our opinions may be of the causes that led .to this war, there is now no room for any differences, as at present we know no party, we are Britons first and party men afterwards. This war has been forced upon us, and it is the duty of men of all parties and creeds to give the Government their solid backing. It natur- ally follows that the discussion of our party measures must stand over until we have won a complete and final victory over the liombastic German. May this be speedily accomplished is the wish of
E. WYNNE JONES, President Progressive Labour League. 540, Knutsford-road, Warrington, August 7th, 1914.

div.head: PARALYSED MARKETS.
div.p: PARALYSED MARKETS.

Sir,—! wonder if the Honorary Secretary of the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society could explain what she means when she says " it is more by luck than good management that there is to be no famine"? Does she think that commerce and finance are left to luck? Again, does she not realise that men and boys would suffer starvation as well as women and girls? Anti-Suffragists do not say that women have' no share in war; what we say is that men are more capable of controlling commerce, finance and war than women would be; and I am quite certain that the vast majority of the women of Great Britain are thankful that, at the present moment, public affairs are controlled by men. What would our feelings be like to-day if we alone of all European Powers were controlled by a majority of women? I think the events of the last few days have proved the impossibility of ever giving women the Imperial vote; though they have not altered the desirability of giving us our fair share of control over domestic, social and moral ques- tions. _ _
GWLADYS GLADSTONE SOLOMON, National League for Opposing Woman Suffrage.
Hamtistead Way, Hendon..

div.head: RUNCORN GUARDIANS. To Relieve Cases Occasioned by the War. THE CLERK AS TERRITORIAL OFFICER.
div.p: RUNCORN GUARDIANS. To Relieve Cases Occasioned by the War. THE CLERK AS TERRITORIAL OFFICER.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. G. Pilling presiding in the absence of the Chairman. The Local Government Board wrote inform- ing the Board that the Governmpnt had consti- tuted a committee, with the President acting as chairman, to advise on the measures neces- sary to deal with any distress that might arise in consequence of the war. It was considered ad- visable that there should be formed throughout the county representative local committees in each borough and urban district, the population of which exceeded 20,000, and in each county, exclusive of these areas, whose function it would be to consider the distribution of ,such relief as might be required. It was intended that Guard- ians should continue to deal with all persons who had been in the habit of relying on Poor Law relief, and that such persons should not receive assistance from the special committees, and should be discouraged from applying for such assistance. Instructions for the formation of the committees were appended. The Chairman (Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun.) was appointed to attend a meeting of the committee at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe. In the event of his not being able to go, Mr. Woodward should take his place. WITHDRAWING CHILDREN.

FARM AND GARDEN.
DANGEROUS WEED SEEDS.

The seeds of weeds are responsible for more mischief than that with which they are usually credited. Poisoning of farm animals, and some- times death, may arise from their constimption in the byrproducts from patent and other foods made from corn of all kinds. This is a danger which has often proved serious abroad, and in foreign cakes—rape, for example—the same thing occurs at times. There can be no doubt that many so-called " weed" seeds contain much good feeding mate- rial, but others are undoubtedly injurious. Among these are Ergot, Corn Cockle, Charlock, Darnel (a wild Rye-grass), Yellow Rabble, Cow Wheat and Rust Spores. Even a meal made up of some of these bad substances has been offered for sale on the Continent. Corn Cockle and Charlock are the most likely to find their way into corn in this country, and poultry- keepers should look out for the former.—" Agri- cultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

div.head: LAMB FOODS.
div.p: LAMB FOODS.

The next two months is a most critical time with lambs. They must be kept thriving and they need as much change of pasture as can be given them, while having nothing of a frothy nature. If there is plenty of meat left in the pastures when they are weaned, the lambs are best left there for a while and fed with well- hearted Cabbage which has been grown for the purpose. This diet can afterwards be continued on stubble or grass fog until Mid-September, when they may be folded on the cabbage pre- paratory to turnips. Clover fog is good for them sometimes, but it must be well grown and dry when the lambs are put on it. We have had difficulty with lambs on clover, but never on cabbage.— Agricultural Economist and Hor- ticultural Review."

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Take cuttings of Violas and Pansies. Do not use flowering stems. Pick dead flowers off Roses, and give each tree a good soaking of liquid manure to encour- age later blooms. Layer Strawberries and water afterwards. Hoe between all plants in flower and vegetable gardens. Propagate Pinks by cuttings, or pipings as they are called. Cut horizontally just below a leaf joint, and nip off the lower leaves. Plant in a shady place in soil to which a liberal por- tion of sand has been added. heer them in a Moist state.
Thin out all worn-out wood of Black Cur- rants. Slorten the side shoots of Red and White Currants. •
If a few mint growths are cut back, it will encourage young growths, which will coaie in useful in the autumn.
After Carnation layers are replanted the old wood need not be discarded if there are two or three good shoots remaining. These will carry a good show of flowers another year. . .

gome Chrysa.nthemums throw up a lot of flower buds in a cluster, and if all the bids are allowed to remain the result is a cluster, of medium-sized flowers. Rub off buds close _to- gether, to allow the remaining buds to expand better.
Give outdoor Tomatoes when the fruits are set a dressing of Superphosphate of Lime, prick- ing it into the surface at the rate .of one table- spoonful to each plant. . . _ _

Sow winter Spinach, Lettuce, Cabbages, Tur- nips, and Red Cabbage. Light pruning of Roses after the first lot of flowers are over will be helpful to the plants in producing finer flowers later on. All the thin weak growths which are incapable of bearing good flowers should be cut off; all shoots that have flowered should be cut back to the first good eye. Earth up strong plants of Brussels sprouts to prevent the wind blowing them about.
A LITTLE-KNOWN ROSE.
Zephyrine Drouldn is, I believe, a hybril

Bout:1)(in rose and a semi-climber ;if I-may coin a word). She throws out great strong shoots, which may be pegged down or trained along a line, and she will go on doing this year after year, with masses of bloom, whether pruned or not. When her clusters of buds are thinned out she presents quite a respectably sized blossom, but, left to herself; each indivi- dual flower is rather small. She has not many petals, and, full bloom, falls almost as loosely as Gustav Regis or a China Rose—almost, but not quite. Her fragrance is as perfect as that of La France, though not quite the same, and her colour is the most pure carmine ,pink in the rose world, deeper than the wild rose, deeper even than the Sweet Briar; the same but in- finitely brighter. In a room she puts all other roses in the shade, and keeps her colour longer than they.—" Agricultural Economist and Hor- ticultural Review." '

div.head: SUNFLOWER SEED.
div.p: SUNFLOWER SEED.

Sunflower seed has io;:s; been known to be valuable by those. versed in the lesser knows food stuffs, and we have confirmation of it from Continental sources, where such seeds are far more in use than they are with us. Sunflower cake is -good dairy food, and is even said to influence the amount of fat, which is very unusual, and this, favourably. Earthnut, Sesame, Palm and . Cocoanut cakes are of a similar nature, and owing to a small ~demand are not expensive, and if fed in moderation they are capable of being very useful, as they are all rich foods; the two first and Sunflower' exceptionally so. Unfortunately, they are not very easy to procure, but Sunflower can be easily grown on poor dry soil, and seems to be just one of those neglected plants which should belong to intensive culture. It is useful for its oil, also for poultry, and ,for various kinds of live stock the form of cake and meal.— " Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

-We are authorised by the Home Secretary 'to' issue the following statement:— "During the lass two days a considerable number of Germans, chiefly reservists, have been arrested in various .parts of the country. "This has been done as a precautionary mea- sure and in accordance with what is usual in

"Those aliens who were known to be spies were arrested early last week; and, thougl,there is at the present moment a clear necessity for taking precautionary measures, the public may rest assured that the great majority of Ger- mans remaining in this cduntry are peaceful and innocent persons from whom no danger is to be feared." As required by the new Aliens Restriction Act, a large number of those of German nation- ality resident in this country have already registered themselves. There were many curious cases. In several instances those registering had not visited Ger- many for more than 50 years, and, professed themselves more English •than the English. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1914.
RESULTS OF BAD MARKETING.

The American Government poultry experts of the Department of Agriculture have issued a statement that .R 9,000,000 a year is lost by care-- less egg handling on American poultry farms. This is 15 per cent. of the annual egg crop, which is valued- at £60,000:000. The Department of Agriculture is endeavouring to induce farmers to pay more attention to their hens, and to reap a larger profit for themselves, while at the same time giving a better quality of•egg to, the con- sumer at less cost. The farmers are accused by the Government of permitting hens to use 'foul houses and nests, of not feeding the birds pro- perly,- and of storing eggs in damp places before marketing them. It is declared that farmers; by using a little of their spare time in attending to their hens, could work a revolution in the re- sults. The hens should not be permitted to hunt for their own living, but should be fed at least once a day in summer and twice a day in winter, when pickings are bad. They should have clean nests, and should be prevented from laying in out-of-the-way places. If these rules are - fol- lowed, the Department of, Agriculture is ready to guarantee more money to the farmers and better eggs to the housewives.

div.head: INHERITANCE AND EGG-LAYING.
div.p: INHERITANCE AND EGG-LAYING.

The schemes of the Utility Poultry Club for a Progeny Laying Test and Investigations con- cerning the Inheritance of the egg-laying powers of poultry have now been approved by the Development Commissioners, and the Treasury have intimated that they will make a grant from the fund, not exceeding .2708 in respect of the work to be done during 1914-15. The Devel- opment Commissioners recognise that the work should be carried on for a period of seven years, and the Treasury intimate their willingness to give the necessary financial support if the posi- tion of the fund permits and the scheme pro- gresses satisfactorily. The estimated cost of the whole scheme is about .25,000. The grant is made subject to cer- tain conditions which the committee find no difficulty in agreeing to, and also to a condition that the club contribute .250 per annum to the expenses of the Progeny Test. This the com- mittee have agreed to do, and propose to make a special appeal for the purpose. Considering the substantial support given to the schemes by the Treasury, this amount ought to be raised from the poultry industry. The club have been fortu- nate in securing the co-operation of Major C. C. Hurst in the carrying out of the schemes. Major Hurst has for some years been conducting at the Burbage Experimental Farm at Hinckley, Leicestershire, some important experiments in the breeding of horses and cattle, and recently he has giiren some attention to poultry. For the due carrying out of the schemes of the club, Major Hurst will be solely responsible. By the Progeny Laying Test an attempt will be made to show in a popular way the results of breeding from good and bad layers for some years in succession. The best and worst layers in the best six pens in tlie present competition will be mated up by the owner of the birds, and from the progeny will be reared a sufficient num- ber of birds to enable another test to be made in ,the same way, a new male bird being again supplied by the owner. In this way the owners of the pens will be able to ,demonstrate their ability in mating. The other part of the scheme is much more ambitious. No experimental work to any large extent has been done in this coun- try to prove how the the egg-laying powers of poultry are transmitted. Dr. Raymond Pearl has conducted nest interesting experiments at the Marine Experiment Station in the U.S.A., and Major Hurst proposes to carry out similar experiments here on a more extended scale. The points upon which information is to be obtained are—

1. To test Dr. Pearl's conclusion in regard to the sex-limited inheritance of high winter yield with two of the best utility strains of white Wyandottes and white Leghorns. 2. To investigate separately the inheritance of prolificacy, weight of egg and colour of egg. From the results obtained from these experi- ments:
3. To determine any correlations or couplings that may exist in the three characters, and whether any correlation exists between these characters and the physical features of the birds.

To carry out the work accurately every bird tested will be separately penned; an expert poul- tryman and boy and a skilled recorder will be continually engaged throughout the experi- ments. Some idea of the magnitude of the work may be gathered when it is estimated that over half a million 'single records will be made in the seven years. These will provide sufficient data to give a definite answer to many questions of great practical and biological interest.

div.head: HARVEST IN ENGLAND Improvement in Cereal Crops. VOLUNTEER AID TO FARMERS.
div.p: THE HARVEST IN ENGLAND Improvement in Cereal Crops. VOLUNTEER AID TO FARMERS.
It is reassuring _says "The Times," ~,to

know that the best informed are the least apprehensive about the security of our food supplies. lln official and other circles familiar with the facts there is complete tranquility. There must be a certain amount of rearrange.. ment of the imports, but no doubt is felt as to the ability to make good from other quarters the consignments of grain from the Baltic and the Blaek Sea. The filling up of the gaps will not necessarily make demands upon the Atlan- tic traffic—including the Indian contribution— which it will be unable to bear. One result of the closing of the North Sea trade will be that cargoes which would have gone to Germany will be intercepted to swell British supplies. Although Germany takes most of her £2,000,000 worth of imported wheat from Russia the quantity that can be diverted to English ports is, not inconsiderable.

Our own harvest goes on steadily, though the heavy rains ix mid-week impeded progress at a critical stage. The delay in carting is not yet serious, though slight discoloration may re- sult; the worst feature is that many of the uncut crops have been badly laid. No harvest elk this sitle of the Atlantic is gathered with fewer hands than that of this cbuntry. Mach- inery is employed wherever practicable, hand mowing being restricted to the crops badly broken by storms. Hand reaping will be fairly common this year, but those employed are mostly over service age, and delay through men joining the colours is not serious.

div.head: How to Help in the Fields.
div.p: How to Help in the Fields.

The best way in which volunteer workers can displace horses or trained men in harvest is in gathering the sheaves into suiall'stacks>or•cocks on the field where they would be secure agaipst wet weather until they could be carted. Under the guidance of an experienced man the helpers would soon acquire the art of stack-building. But it should be remembered that harvest/work is practicable only in fine weather, and it would be wise to communicate with farmers before proceeding to their assistance. There is no ground for impatience in the har- vesting of the crops beyond the ordinary desire to save them from undue exposure. As far as the supply and markets are concerned both the grower and the consumer can view the situa- tion with equanimity. The intervention of the Government in regulating prices should satisfy both on this point, while it will prevent specu- lative buying by middlemen. Very little of the new crop has been threshed, but in the country as in the town the first excitement of the war has subsided. Farmers do not welcome official interference, but they will be content with reasonable prices when they recognise that the Government have been moved to intervene on national grounds. Such measures of con- trol as are likely to be imposed will entail little inconvenience either in the harvesting or the marketing of the crops.

div.head: OUR FOOD SUPPLY.
div.p: OUR FOOD SUPPLY.
Government Action to Get the Best Results.

In view of the special importance at the pre- sent time of (securing 'that the home-grown supplies of food-stuffs are used to the best ad- vantage in the public interest, with due regard to future requirements, the President of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries has ap- pointed the following gentlemen to serve as a Consultative Committee: The Right Hon. Sir Ailwyn Fellowes (chairman), Messrs. Charles Bathurst, M.P., Charles•Bidwell, H. Trustram Eve, S. W. Farmer, C. B. Fisher, E. M. Nun- neley, Francis H. Padwick, George Scoby, G. C. Smyth-Richards, R. Stratton, the Hon. Edward G. Strutt, and Mr. Christopher Turner. The first meeting of the committee was held on Monday afternoon at .the .offices of the Sur- veyors' Institution, 12, Great George-street, Westminster, to which address any communi- cations may be sent to Op joint secretaries.

div.head: SUPPLY OF MEAT.
div.p: SUPPLY OF MEAT.

The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries have made special inquiries by their own officers into the supply of meat now in cold Vorage in the principal centfes in England and Wales. As regards chilled and frozen meat, the ex- isting stocks are sufficient to meet the ordin- ary needs at 'the normal rate 'of consumption for about six weeks, while there are three to four weeks' supply on passage and due to arrive shortly. _ _

As regards home supplies, which repregent 60 per cent. Of the total consumption, the Board have ascertained from the recently collected agricultural returns that there is .a substantial increase in the numbers of live stock as com- pared with last year.

div.head: WORK ON WASTE LAND.
div.p: WORK ON WASTE LAND.

The Development Commissioners desire to suggest to landowners in England and Wales that they should at once forward to the Agri- cultural College for ,their Province particulars qf any waste land Which they are willing to place at the disposal of suitable authorities for improvement by such means as reclamation or afforestation. The particulars of the land should include situation,, approximate area, elevation, character of the soil, and the terms on which the land can be obtained by an authority willing to improve it.

CULTIVATION OF VEGETABLES. The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries ap- peal to horticulturists, both owners of private gardens and market gardens, to preserve for distribution to allotment holders and cottagers their surplus stocks of seedling vegetables suit- able for autumn planting in the district. These seedling plants, usually destroyed after ~the growers' own requirements have been satisfied, might under present conditions prove most ; useful. It is suggested that the owners of private gardens should distribute their surplus ; plants locally, either direct or through relief committees. There is a second direction in which horti- culturists, both professional and amateur, might give timely assistance. Much might be accomplished if the gardeners employed in ; private establishments and skilled amateur horticulturists would volunteer to give practi- cal hints on the cultivation of vegetables to the relatively inexperienced people who will endea- vour to eke out their resources in the coming year by resorting to the cultivation of the allot- ments provided for them by agencies formed to combat the hardships caused by unemployment. Although there are large stocks of food in the country, it is the duty of every occupier of land to avoid waste, and by forethought and consideration of the needs of others to age- viate the hardships that ,a rise in the price of food-stuffs will entail.

div.head: CYCLISTS' NOTEBOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLISTS' NOTEBOOK.
Independence That the Cycle 'Brings. RIDES WITH AN OBJECT.

Beeston Castle.—Most peple seek this place via Torporley. It is a mistake, for the best view of the castle is obtained from the north- west. Therefore cross the Forest tp Tarvin, and at the church take the' Torporley-road, and the Castle is in view almost all the way through,' Burton and Huxley. The great lonely cliff is al fine sight as the plain is crossed from the lastl village. At Horton's Mill great care is needed in crossing the Canal Bridge. The (castle itself •is one of the finest of the kind I know in the north, Middleham Castle, near Ripon, the home of the King-maker, only exceeding our present ruins in size. It is closed on Tuesday, Thurs- day and Sunday, and if it was in national hands the arrangements for the comfort of visitors would be vastly implroved, as they ought to be. The view from the top on August Monday was a magnificent one. From Moe! Famma in Den- , bigh to the Cat and Fiddle on the Derbyshire border is 52 miles, and from the Shropshire Wrekin to Rivington Pike is 65. All these points were clearly visible; so were Stretton Church and Warrington smoke, the New Brigh- ton Tower and Chester, with its cathedral, and Eaton Hall. The doorway to the castle is an interesting structure; the well and the caves are always open to visitors. A good pathway runs round the base of the hill, througli the wood, though at present interrupted by a score of uprooted trees, damaged in last year's cyclone. Near the teahouse is one of the finest walnut trees I have ever seen, well charged with fruit. But for the points in architecture, his- tory, &c., the Warrington Reference Library contains many guide-books, which should be consulted.

div.head: POINTS FOR CYCLIST.
div.p: POINTS FOR CYCLIST.

The latter half of Air: Fra-nii—Ho-w-den's book consists of 21 short chapters dealing with cycling in all its aspects. It has been brought up to date in a way worthy of its author. He starts with a chapter on choosing a cycle, warn- ing the tyro against the advertising dodges about "slightly soiled bicycles at one-third of their value—owner had a trap accident, or going abroad." Why anyone cannot spare an extra shilling or two, to pay an agent in town who has a reputation to lose, to choose a cycle that will fit him or her, and that is not made of gas pipe tubing., &c., is past the wit of anyone to under- stand. And the end of the season will see hun- dreds of these worthless cyclei put on 'the market. All the more so this year on account of the turmoil and the upset in that same market.

div.head: Freedom of the Cycle.
div.p: Freedom of the Cycle.

The book deals, --among other points, with three-speed gears, tyres, lamps, gear cases, brakes, cleaning, oiling, learning to ride, cycling for ladies, touring. The last word of the book is quoted froth "linklos," that prince of modern cyclists:—

div.head: WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON BURIAL SOCIETY.

The members .of the above society assembled at the British Workman Dining Rol:1ms, Horse- market-street, on Monday, .to , celebrate the 43rd anniversary of the society. The Presi- dent (Mr. William E. Clegg) presided, and was supported by the Vice-president (Mr. Peter L. Edgar), Mr. James Parr (treasurer), Messrs. William EckersleS,, James •Gresty and Joseph Adams (trustees), Mi. Laurence Weir (general secretary) and others. The Chairman ex- pressed the pleasure it gave him to preside over such a large and enthusiastic gathering, who, he felt sure, would appreciate the financial position of the society and the headway it had made during the past year.—The General Sec- retary presented the annual balance sheet, which showed that the society's funds now amounted to S-5,241 Bs. 91(1., as compared with £5,007 10s. 21d. for the previous year, a gain of £233 18s. 7d. There was a membership Of 1;555. The report further showed that the ,society had paid away in death claims £lll 55., as compared With £77 15s. the year previous, and that they :had invested in the Warrington Corporation and bn mortgage £4,6Bo.—The auditors, in giving their report, found the col- lectors'- books, the general register and the general secretary's ledger in perfect order and correct; also the treasurer's book correct and satisfactory. The lank book, Corporation bonds, mortgage investments and vouchers were produced for inspection, and the same were duly vouched.—Through a difficult year the society has made steady progress financially, and has maintained its membership in numerical strength, and thus affords encouragement for renewed and increased efforts for the progress of the society. The permanent officials were thanked for their courtesy and assistance.— Mr. Jaines T. Barton was elected president for the ensuing year, and Mr. John T. Baskerville vice-president. Mr. John Haley was elected auditor for the next two years.—A very inter- esting programme was gone through affecting the general welfare of the members, and the following took part in the discussion: Messrs. John Haley, William Eckersley, Joseph Porn- hey, Joseph Adams, Frederick Massey, James T. Barton and others.—A vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring President (Mr. Wil- liam E. div.head: MOTOR 'BUS AND RURAL DEPOPULATION
div.p: MOTOR 'BUS AND RURAL DEPOPULATION

The motor 'bus has penetrated the heart of the country and brought Something of the ex- hilarating life of the town to the doors of a re- mote peasantry. People who hitherto never went anywhere can now, for a few pence, not only indulge in an invigorating "joy-ride," but can get a better market for their produce. The 'bus also bring l igore visitors into the country, and the visitors 'bring an interest as well as money. This innovation, rather than increas- ing discontent 'among the village folk, has in- spired a greater contentment. It has bred a fuller life. Because they can run into town whenever they desire to do so the craving wears off. It is only when the city seems so unattain- able that it is so enchanting. And I believe that the proposed establishment of a motor 'bus ser- vice in rural districts throughout the country will eventually do more for the contentment and prosperity of the farming community than any- thing has ever done since the first railroad was laid down.—" Agricultural Economist and Horti- cultural Review."

div.p: THE FALSE NEWS SCANDAL. Hon .01fenders May Be Punished.
It is to be hoped that this country is not to be afflicted with a crop of false statements such as the one from which we suffered' during the Boer War.

In the House of Commons on Saturday, Mr. Joy-nson-Hicko asked the Home Secretary whe- ther his attention had been called to the state- ment in a special edition of a daily 'wiper that Morning in regard to a naval battle off Holland, which appeared to be untrUe in every detail, and whether the Government could take some steps—(cheers)—to Prevent a newspaper of this importance from publishing infamous false- hoods, which caused great inconvenience, hard- ship, and heartburnings, in order that people might be deluded into purchasing copies of the paper. It was infamous conduct. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McKenna: I learn from the Admiralty that there is no foundation whatever for the statement that there has been a great naval battle. This House, I am sure, will join in the condemnation in the strongest terms of the fab- rication of false news, which I cannot say, and do not say, was in this case wilfully done, but which might be wilfully done, to assiet the,cir- culation of a newspaper. (Hear, hear.)

In answer to Mr. Lawson- .. Mr. McKenna stated that as the Press Bureau had been formed the public had a reasonable right to expect that no news would be published in the Press except such as was .furnished by the Bureau. The -organisation would be in operation from to-day. The law was already strong enough to deal with such questions, but the difficulty of proof was extremely great. The National Liberal Federation on Saturday issued the following circular to the affiliated associations of England and Wales:— " Dear Sir,—lt seems fitting that we should inform the' affiliated Liberal Associations of England and Wales that from the moment when war was declared the party propaganda of the National Liberal Federation has been suspended arid will remain suspended indefi- nitely. While war is being waged the voice of party should be silenced. • The immediate duty of all good citizens is to sink their political differences in support of the King's Government and to render such service as each can best perform in movements which know no party distinction,

• "Members and officials of Liberal Associa- tions will doubtless give themselves freely to such non-party work as they find ready to their hands in connection with the relief of distress and the regulation of food supplies, and the other kindred movements, local or national, which the exigencies of the hour are calling into existence. In these .works of necessity. div.head: Needs of the Men.
div.p: Needs of the Men.

There were, first of all, the requirements of the men going to fight and serve the countiy. The bachelors—the young men—would be re- instated when they came home—and they car- ried their responsibilities, more or less, under their own hats... They would receive pay, and he did not think there was any particular need to think they would require substantial assistance. In regard to the married men, he hoped and believed that firms generally in the town would do what some firms were doing' to see that the wives at home could keep the home together without anxiety whilst their husbands were away._ _ _
With regard to the injured, it was impossible to say with any certainty whether Warrington was going to suffer at all, or very much, but de- pendents would receive compensation for losses sustained.

div.head: .States Liability.
div.p: The .States Liability.

On that score the Government, in their pro- posal to allocate £300,000,000 to the cost of the war, stated that that money would be applied, amongst other things, to the relief of widows and dependents of those killed in action. In the House of Commons', after the terrible dis- aster to the Amphion, .the Prime Minister turned round and said that no time would be lost in seeing that the dependents of those lost would be' provided for. (Applause.) They did not want to do things twice over. They paid taxation to the State. Such things 'ere a national liability and not improperly met out of the National Purse to which they all con- tributed. If the State was going to take that duty on its shoulders, he was not quite sure whether it would not fall heavily on the shoulders of those who paid taxes. That was a matter of which they would learn more as time went on.

An Optimist. Then there uas the question of unemploy- ment. He was an optimist and he did not think there was going to be any unemployment. They must not forget that a great number of the men who were at present employed were going to the front, and their places would have to be filled by others. It was a matter of experience that during the last three years, 111) to quite recently, when they had been approach- ing a period of trade depression" there had been no lack of employment in the town. He could assure them that it had been no easy thing to get men, and, he thought, that was pretty general amongst employers of labour in the town. There might be some trades—certainly he was the last to attempt to speak for all trades in Warrington—that might be affected. On the other hand, he was of the opinion that before long trades would be carried on quite as busily and actively as ever before. Just for the moment there had been considerable dis- turbance in business, owing to difficulties in effecting shipments. Merchants who had bought goods had been faced with advanced freights and heavy insurance against war risks. That, in view • of the critical position in which the whole of the commercial activity of the world had been thrown, had caused merchants to sus- pend shipments, and a great many of them had suffered considerable inconvenience, even to closing down works, or, at least, certain depart- ments.

div.head: Prosperity for Iron Trade.
div.p: Prosperity for Iron Trade.

. _ He, however, believed that in about a fort- night the trade routes of the world would be so clear that they would be able to ship to any part of the world. He was confident, if that came about, that the iron and steel trade would be so great that it would be quite out of the capacity of the country to meet the demand. They had suffered in the past from competition with Germany of a most serious character, and everyone knew their production had been reaching the neighbourhood of 18,000,000 tons a year to the 6,000;000 or 8,000,000 tons of England. They had no steel trade of any magnitude with the Continent; it was chiefly with the Far East, the Colonies, America and Canada. All these markets were open, and would be open to them. That which had been the production of Germany would be knocked on the head during the war, if not for a longer period, and he thought that in a very .short time the iron and steel trade of this country would be more than that with 'which the manufacturers would he able to deal. He was confident that the iron and steel works of WarNngton‘ would be able to keep -going, and he hoped they would be kept busy to the ad- vantage of the town. (Hear, hear.)

The Cotton Industry. He thought that there had been suffering in the cotton industry—although there was only one cotton firm in Warrington—owing to de- pression which set in before the war.' He did hot think the latest developments had anything to do with it. With the ordinary course of trade it would recover. Possibly, with the absence of German competition, it would be lifted out of the slough of despond.. (Hear, hear.)

He was most hopeful from all points of view that if employers did their best there would be no dislocation, and he urged them to work men on short time rather than discharge a number. The employment in Warrington. in a few months would be on a level which they might, at all ievents, not regard as unsatisfactory. (Hear, hear.) Having regard to those con- siderations he was very hopeful that the calls on the fund from Warrington and the activi- ties of the committee would not be great. He would hasten to say, however, that they welcomed the appointment of the committee, and they thought it a desirable thing to create the machinery with which to deal with emer- gencie 'slould, they arise. SUNDAY OF INTERCESSION.

Last Sunday, "the first Sunday since the opening of war, was observed as one of peculiar solemnity by Christians of all denominations. Special prayers were offered for the success of our arms and for the triumph of right and justice. A form of Public Intercession had been pre- pared by -authority, and the Archbishops and Bishops had authorised its use, as the fore- runner of other forms of prayer for interces- sory services of various kinds. The National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches have arranged a series of daily prayer meetings to be held at the Memorial Hall, Far- ringdon-street, E.C., at noon. These meetings are entirely undenominational, and will be conducted by leaders of all denominations. In the whole of the Warrington churches and chapels the keynote to Sunday's texts was the war, and it was announced in a number of them that to-morrow's collections would be given to the Prince of Wales' National Fund. Special prayers were offered for the protection of the forces of the -Crown, and hymns befitting the occasion were sung.

art in Heaven, hallowed be Thy Name." There .was only one subject uppermost in everybody's mind at the present time, and that subject was the War. When one vonsidered their test it was tragic to remember that the same prayer was being offered in all the countries which were in deadly conflict.

_ One great theologian had suggested that "Oar Father" did not adequately express the love of God towards man, and substituted in its place the idea of motherhood, and therefore spoke of God as "our great mother." He had heard sisters use the sacred name of mother, and then, in a' drunken brawl, disfigure each other's faces. They belonged to that class known as the Submerged Tenth, whose ideal of mother- hood was very low. Now they saw the nations in deadly conflict, speaking of God as the Great Mother, but what portion of the nations were the Submerged Tenth? • It was remarkable that all the nations in strife were acknowledged to be Christian nations, and when they recollected again that all of them spoke of God as "Our Father which art in Heaven," .they, for a moment, lost faith in the human race. .

A detachment of the Army Service Corps, under the command of Lieutenant H. Fair. dough, attended St. Paul's Church on Sunday morning, and the Rev. William Braceeamp— the chaplain—in the course of his sermon, said he was delighted to see his comrades there. The visit was appreciated,especially, as was known perfectly well, when their orders were such that they might be sent for at any moment. To the general congregation he had only one word to say—the time of preaching was past, for they had with them the time of prayer—and it was that they should humble themselves and appreciate the services of the Church. Many of thenr would not be able to go to the front, but they could help in other ways, and pray to Almighty God to guide our soldiers and sailors. Speaking to the soldiers, the Chaplain said the text—" Ye shall not fear them; for the Lord your God He shall fight for you" (Deut 22)—was the one he gave to their mates in the Drill Hall the previous afternoon—truly, if the Lord was on their side all would be right. If they looked at the children of Israel they would find that every time they went forth to battle in the name of the Lord they succeeded and every time they went on their own they met with defeat.

div.head: "UPHOLD THE HONOUR OF THE COUNTRY."
div.p: "UPHOLD THE HONOUR OF THE COUNTRY."

"We believe," said the Chaglain, "our battle is absolutely right, that we have been forced, and now it is for us to uphold the honour of our country. You must be prepared, if needs be, even to lay down your lives, and if you go forth with the Lord on your side, realising that God will fight your battles, you are bound to succeed. "I want you all to feel that the credit of the nation rests upon you; therefore be absolutely straight in all your actions, and absolutely loyal to your superiors. " They should remember that the Kink of kings would give them the victory, provided they stuck to Him. He would like them also to. remember that they at St. Paul's Church would be praying for them every night at eight o'clock, and he wanted the soldiers to think of them.

"We will take as much care as we possibly n of your wives and children, and we shall never forget you in our prayers. My last word to you as your Chaplain is 'Go forth, God be with you, and God bless you.'"

He had striven to see how Eng- land could remain neutral in the crisis. It was his opinion, and he held it very humbly as a pronounced advocate of peace, that when Bel- gian territory was violated, mere diplomatic support by the English Government was impoit• sible.

The cause of the trouble was not far to seek— the three Emperors and their immediate mili- tary cliques were absolutely responsible for the European conflagration. It would have been a happy ending to the quarrel if the prime cause, the three Emperors and their cliques, had been compelled to settle it by a life and death fight amongst themselves. One rejoiced to remember that in this matter the hands of our King were clean.

Mr. Ogden said that had been a breathless week, and it would be well to remember at these times that there was a brotherhood of nations. and that God had made all people of one blood. In these times, when English feeling was roused against their German cousins, it should be re- membered that what happened in war was no criterion as to what- happened in peace. They could not forget that the Germans were a Teuton people—the fair hair and blue eyes told their own tale. They could not denounce the Tenton, because, in so doing, they would de- nounce themselves. Ile had sat in the homes of German people, and he would never forget their hospitality. A Berlin crowd smashes the British Embassy and sings " Deutehland, Deutchland "; an English crowd wrecks a German's shop and howls "Rule, Britannia:" Right down to the bottom of their national life both nations were the same. The 'English wife clings to her husband as he is called to the colours, it casts a great shadow over the home; the German mother bids fare- well to her boy and strokes his flaxen-hair, be is only a lad of 18, but she will never see him again. There was the same shadow over the English and the German homes, there was the same poignant suffering. Let them all remember, however, that that was a war of the autocrats, and when it was over let them all seek to foster a common under- standing with the workers and those responsible for national affairs, in what must be a very sad land across the North Sea. div.head: VAR.
div.p: THE VAR.

Perhaps it may be unnecessary again to refer to the clear conscience and the clean hands with which Great Britain has answered the insolent and callous challenge of the GERMAN EMPEROR; but when we can prove our case out of the mouth of our adver- saries it is usually worth while to do so. As we know from SIR EDWARD GREY, the Germans asked us to abuse the trust of Belgitlm and betray the 1 interests of France in such a manner that we should have inflicted upon ourselves a disgrace from which the good name of this country would never have recovered. We now have before ' us a speech of the GERMAN CHANCELLOR in the Reichstag, made on August 4th, before we had declared war, in which I he unblushingly said: ; We are now in a state of necessity, and necessity knows no law! Our troops have occu- pied Luxemburg, and perhaps are already on Belgian soil. Gentlemen, that is contrary to the dictates of international law. It is true that the French Government has declared at Brussels that France is willing to respect the neutrality of Belgium as long as her opponent respects it. We knew, however, that France stood ready, for the invasion. France could wait, but we could not wait. A French move- ment upon our flank Upon the lower Rhine Might have been disastrous. So we were com- pelled to override the just protest of the Luxem- burg and Belgian Governments. The wrong— r speak openly—that we are committing we will endeavour to make good as soon as our military goal has been reached. Anybody who is threat- ened, as we are threatened, and is fighting for his highest possessions can have only one thought—how he is to hack his way through. And so, wrong as it admittedly Was, the German hordes began to hack their way through. But in these days there are others than Germans who a. re adepts at the hacking business. The necessity that knew no law in this case Was that Germany Should be in France before Russia wasP ready to strike. And Germany, being unable to face the forts on the French frontier, had decided to sneak in by the back 'door provided by Belgium and Luxemburg. But the Germans reckoned without their Belgians and their Liege. Now they have been effectually held up by Belgium, in as glorious a period as graces the national life of any people in history, the Germans have lost the , advantage for which they threw away their honour and ensured the active hostility of Great Britain: Instead of raiding France they are fighting for their lives in Belgium, and the Allies have little fear of the ultimate result. Delay is fatal to German hopes for more reasons than one. Germany's enemies are closing upon her more effectually as the result of each day gained. She is practically isolated; and we have only to think of the dis- location in business and the disaster that was threatening in our own country last week to understand what a prolonged war will mean to a country for whom sea communications are almost wholly closed. German finan- cial experts, who have calculated in quiet times the staying power of Ger- many, have calculated that 3,000,000 men could be kept in the field for six months, but beyond that appears to be like a glance taken at the space that L lies beyond the clouds.
THE MAN WHO KEEPS HIS HEAD.
l" Britain's Motto: Business as Usual."—H. E. Morgan.)

There's a man who fights for England. and he'll keep her still atop. He will guard her from dishonour in the market and the shop, He will save her homes from terror on the fields of Daily Bread, He's the man who sticks to business, he's the man who keeps his head.

Let the foe who strikes at England hear her wheels of commerce turn, Let the ships that war with England see her factory furnace burn; For the foe most fears the cannon, and his heart most quails with dread, When behind the man in khaki is the man who keeps his head.

Brand him traitor and assassin who with miser's coward mood Has his gold locked up in secret and his larders stored with food, Who has cast adrift his workers, who lies sweating in his bed, And who snarls to hear the laughter of the man who keeps his head.

Let the poor min teach the rich man, for the poor man's constant strife Is from day to day to seek work, day by day to war with life, And the poor man's home hangs ever by a frail and brittle thread, And the poor man's often hungry, but the poor man keeps his head.

When the ships come back from slaughter, and the troop; march home from war; When the havoc strewn behind us threats the road that lies before, Every hero shall be welcomed, every orphan shall be fed, By the man•who stuck to business, by the man who kept his head. HAROLD BEGBIE.

TO FIGHT POSSIBLE DISTRESS.
PUBLIC WORK TO BE UNDERTAKEN.

There was a large and representative gather- ing of leading Warrington citizens on. Monday night, called by the Mayor to lay plans to meet any, possible distress that the war may entail upon the town. The cool resolve with which the meeting entered upon the task was typical of our national spirit at its best—it was hoped, and believed, that we shall recover our normal state before the shock to business has had time to do very much mischief; but we are determined to take no risks, and the machinery Was set up by which the evils of war may, in the worst eventuality, be mini- mised. 1 t was, decided to make an appeal to the town for • contributions to a relief fund opened by the Mayor in support of the National Relief Fund opened Lby His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and a representative com- mittee was appointed to allocate the grants which will be made from that fund for local PurPoSes. A local fund was suggested, but, as Mr. Felix Maginn says, this appeal to the generosity of the public is a national affair and is not bounded by parochial limitations.

The Mayor, who at the town's meeting read conditions under which Corporation employes will enter upon military duties, conditions which revealed our local governors in the light of model employers, announced at the Council meeting the following night that the General Purposes Committee had decided to push on all public Work if employment were needed owing to the war, ineluding the laying out of the extension of Victoria. Park with the lake that the Latehford Ward representatives " de- sired so much."

TIIE QUESTION OF EMPLOYMENT. We are bound to have loss and suffering a.,iong those engaged in the actual fighting and their relatives. That will be remedied, as far as money can make good, such domestic calamities. The immediate question is to see that the distress that may result from unem- ployment and scarcity does not unduly afflict the town. Mr. W. Peter Bylands, speaking as one of the heads of the iron trade, does not contentplate that that industry, which in War- rington finds employment for a good portion of its workmen, will suffer more than a tem- porary set-back. He gave his reasons for thinking so, reasons which seemed to justify the optimism which his words revealed. All, of course, depends upon the ability—the cer- tain ability, we hope—of the British, French, and, perhaps, the Japanese, Navies to open all the trade routes of the world to British ship- ping, with the result that the whole of our trade, except with Germany and Austria, will go on as usual. The iron and steel trade stands actually to gain something by the war, for Germany, our greatest competitor, in this branch of commerce, will be worse than idle— she will be employed in turning her plough- shares into swords. If she were not her overseas trade would be stopped completely by the same Navies that keep the seas open to us. Such considerations as tliese make Mr. Itylands confident that in a' fdrtnight we shall enter upon such a period of activity in the steel and iron trade that it will be quite beyond the capacity of the country to meet the demand.

SHORT TIME AS TEMPORARY EXPEDIENT. Other trades that have been adversely affected by the sudden rise in freights and insurance charges on shipping, and the uncer- tainties of war may be similarly affected for the better when the Fleet has established its supremacy, but what shall be done in the meantime? The best suggestion that has been made is that the burden of • unemployment should be distributed as equally as possible. The whole of the men in a works should be put on short time in preference to the device of discharging some; that will ensure the pre- vention of extreme poverty and keep the men available for any sudden reversion of trade to its normal state. What we ought to do may be illustrated by a case showing what we ought not to do. Mr. Williams, the Board of Trade lofficial, instanced the case of an employer who had discharged 300 men and sent £5,000 to the Prince of Wales' Fund. It is fairly clear that ,f 5,000 spent upon employ- ing 300 men would be far more profitably .used, both to the individuals and the nation, than by throwing out of work 300 men and spending £5,600 in charity. If it is true that we only need to make an effort to tide us over the first few weeks of the war, there ought to be no difficulty in doing that.

div.head: AN AUXILIARY FUND.
div.p: AN AUXILIARY FUND.

It was understood, at the meeting that should distress assert itself locally at a later, period in a volume so great as to need more assist- ance than could be expected from the National Fund, a local fund would be opened. It was announced by Councillor Henry Roberts, who expressed his plea:sure at meeting so optimistie a person as Mr, flylands at the present time, and hinted that we were in for a• very much bigger job than some of us were aware of, that his firm—Messrs. -Joseph Crostleld and Sons— had sent £l,OOO to the National Fund, and Sir Gilbert Greenall declared his intentiOn of giv= ing a like sum. Other promises .of £lOO a month and £5O a month for live months. seem to have been conditional upon local needs subsequently proving themselves to be of a substantial nature---,about which, as we have said, there appears to be some doubt at present. In the meantime we have to concentrate upon supporting the National Fund, from which we shall have what help the committee require; .and if we do not require a purely local fund because of our comparative prosperity, our prosperity should make us the more willing to contribute something towards the wants of those Other districts that will not participate in the diversion of some of Germany's iron trade to this country.

NECESSITOUS CHILDREN TO BE FED. When the Act which provides for the feeding of school children was passed it was provided that food should be given only during such times as the schools were open.. The reason for this is clear. It was an Act' to ensure that children should be in a fit physical condition to receive the instruction that a compulsory system of education forced upon them. Holi- days and week-ends are free from mental strain; and it was decided that there was no call for a public supply of food at such times. The wisdom of this conclusion has been vigorously questioned, though there can be little doubt that, as an educational affair, the conclusion is absolutely sound and logical. Now, however, the war has intervened, and the Government have decided that necessitous children of school age shall be fed at all times, whether in or out of school hours. Coun- cillor Henry Roberts, who, as chairman of the Education Committee, made this announce- ment to the Council on Tuesday night, thought the Government might have gone further and included adults as well as children in the new arrangements. But there are some matters 1 In which it is advisable to hasten slowly.

div.head: STIRRING WEEK.
div.p: A STIRRING WEEK.

Warrington has done' its share nobly and well. Here we have collected 'all the reserves that were available for the South Lancashires ; here we, have found a full battalion of Terri- torials to volunteer for active service; here we have sworn in large numbers for Kitchener's second army; and we have promised and sup- plied an ample number of ambulance men, nurses and similar auxiliaries for war. When our citizen soldiers departed on Thursday „for a destination that must remain unpublished they went out quietly and determinedly. There was no shouting—they simply went out to do their duty. It follows that the town must and will do its duty.

div.head: TIIE ABSENCE OF PANIC.
div.p: TIIE ABSENCE OF PANIC.

Whatever disposition there was last week to give way to panic has almost disappeared. Trade is steadily re-asserting itself under the safeguards and encouragements that the Gov- ernment are affording, seconded by the good I common-sense of the people themselves. In Warrington many of the works—such as Bylands' and Whitecross—are actually busier as a result of the war, and normal conditions are being reached in most directions, notably in the tanning trade, in which a long-drawn- out strike has come to an end. Iloliday- makers are once again looking seaward, and the railway companies are beginning to realise that there will be a sufficient number of holiday-makers to justify a resumption of the cheap booking facilities. In the Park to-morrow and in the Hippodrome sacred music will be rendered in aid of local war funds.

div.head: GET OUT OF DEBT.
div.p: GET OUT OF DEBT.

Some are asking for "cash" as the basis of their trading, but actual experience proves that this stipulation is not nearly so serious as it looks. No regular customer with an account that is " squared" as a rule at the proper time has been touched by this rule—it is intended to counteract the schemes of those who would run up long scores, people who are a plague to trade in the best of circumstances. We would urge it as a partiotic duty of those who have overdue accounts owing to trades- men to- pay up promptly. They will be serv- ing their country well by getting rid of old debts and thus ceasing to abuse the credit system by which we so largely live.

'Church Lads' Brigade Camp. Daily on 'Saturday morning the Warrington Battalion C.L.B. returned home after a week's camp at Prestatyn. The declaration of war drained the camp of many officers and men, but, nevertheless, the 2,009 under canvas— about 50 from Warrington—enjoyed the life. Major Corah was in command. Adjutant and Captain J. Sankey and Lieutenant Isherwood accompanied the Warrington contingent. Sergeant Dayus's tent was successful in ob- taining Colonel Appleton's prize for the best tent, and also the "Brigade" battalion prize for the cleanest tent in the line. The War- rington lads took a deep interest in the camp sports and with such success that ten prizes were divided amongst the following four local N.C.O.'s: Colour-Sergeant Pinson, Colour. Sergeant Dayus, Sergeant Appleton, and Cor- poral Spencer.

div.head: Death of Mr. James Richardson.
div.p: Death of Mr. James Richardson.

The death ofMr.James Richardson, of Palmyra House, Springfield-street, was an- nounced on Wednesday. Mr. Richardson. who was 64 years of age, had, owing to the delicate state of his health, been staying in North Wales, spending the last fortnight at Rhyl. On Tuesday evening he went to an entertainment, and at about 12.30 a.m., when he arrived at his apartments, he was taken ill and died at nine o'clock from angina pectoris. He was a member of the firm of Messrs. W. and J. Richardson, coal merchants, Marson-street. He was a Churchman. being identified with St. Paul's! He was also a member of the Warrington Cricket Club and a staitnch Conservative. His wife and brother predeceased him last year. He leaves two daughters (married) and one son, who is in the Army Service Corps. The funeral will take place at noon to-day, when a proces- sion will leave Springfield-street at 11.30 a.m., and a service will be conducted at St. Paul's Church at 11.45, after which the interment will take place at the Cemetery.

div.head: AN HISTORIC METING.
div.p: AN HISTORIC METING.
WILLING TO FIGHT BRITAIN'S BATTLES IN A FOREIGN LAND.
Unbounded Enthusiasm.

The historic meeting which was held in the Parr Hall late on Tuesday night will never be forgotten by those who took a part, for it was then that the 4th Battalion South Lancashire (Territerial) Regiment agreed, almost to a man, to offer Itself for foreign service.

div.head: SCENE.
div.p: THE SCENE.

The composition of the assembly was entirely military. In the body of the hall several com- panies were accommodated, whilst others found a foothold in the galleries and on the stage, the tiers leading to the organ being occupied by the officers. The organist's seat was converted into a plat- form, and from this lofty stand Captain Cros- field addressed the men and finally asked them as a battalion if they were willing to help in foreign service. The answer was spontaneous, all bands shot up like so many rifles being shouldered. A momentary pause followed, but it was the lull before the storm, for aft& the fraction of a minute's quietness, the whole body burst into a mighty cheer, and cheers and cheers and cheers followed, each one surpassing in volume its forerunner. The men were enthusi- astic, and applauded the name of the King and "dear old England." • This is the spirit that has helped to build the structure of our Empire—a spirit as warm now as in the days of Drake and Nelson, and Wel- lington and Clive. Not content with this, how- ever, Captain Crosfield challenged each company individually, and as each unmistakably showed its approval, the whole battalion cheered, and cheered again, until one thought that the world was composed of nothing but cheers! At the•conclusion,.when all had signified their willingness, enthusiasm ran high, and hats were thrown aloft to mingle with the applause. The Chaplain's address was well received, and as the officers attempted to leave the stage they were swept off their feet, hoisted upon well-set shoulders and carried, some to the Drill Hall and some even to Orford Barracks, the crowd, on the march, singing patriotic hymns, includ- ing "Rule, Britannia." Yes, "the Warringtons" were not content to defend their country, they were eager to go abroad, to fight there the battles of their native land.

div.head: CHAPLAIN'S WISH. Territorials Join heartily in a Religious Service.
div.p: THE CHAPLAIN'S WISH. Territorials Join heartily in a Religious Service.

Contrary to expectation, the battalion was not called upon to leave Warrington on Saturday, but in preparation of such an event occurring a religious service was held in the Drill Hall on Saturday afternoon. This was conducted by the Chaplain, the Rev. W. Bracecamp, and proved of an impressive character. If they wished to be successful they must have the Lord on their side, said the Chaplain, in the course of his address. A great deal depended upon the men in their individual life, for they must play the game, and obey to the very letter those in command. They should not neglect that, for they would be more successful than if they went their own way. He regretted that he had not been called up, but he would think about them, and they could rest assured that their wives and children would be eared for. Every night whilst they were away a service of intercession would be held in St. Paul's Church at eight o'clock, when they would pray for their success. At that time, concluded the chaplain, think of what is being done for you, and it will help you.

LOCAL M.P.'s BEST WISHES. At the close of the service Colonel Fairclough read a telegram from Mr. Harold Smith, my., tendering his best wishes to the "officers, N.C.O.'s and men on their departure." A similar service was held in the Parr Hall.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC SERVICE._
div.p: ROMAN CATHOLIC SERVICE._

The Catholic members of the battalion at- tended services at the Drill Hall and the Gym- nasium, where .the Rev. Father Swarbreck, accompanied by Fathers Jackson, Huggins and Dolan, assured the men that the Holy Church would pray for them during the war. Those left behind would remember those at the front in their prayers, and for the present wished them "God-speed."

div.head: EAGER CADETS.
div.p: EAGER CADETS.
C.L.B. Offer the War Office 20,000 Men and Boys.
WARRINGTON'S SHARE.

Field Marshal Lord Grenfel, the Governor of the Church Lads' Brigade, has offered to the War Office the whole brigade, numbering over 20,000, the majority of whom are Cadets recog- nised by the Government, and 40 per cent, of whom are over 17 years of age. Officers com- manding units are ordered to report themselves to the local Territorial Association. The offer was only made last week-end, and whilst await- ing its acceptance by the War Office, officers have reported themselves to the various Terri- torial headquarters. Major Brooks (now in command of the Warrington Battalion C.L.8.) is amongst those who have reported themselves.

div.head: POINTS EXPLAINED.
div.p: THE POINTS EXPLAINED.

The facts were disclosed to the members of the St. Elphin's and St. Clement's Companies on Monday, and the St. Paul's Company on Tuesday, and the boys showed an eagerness to do what lay in their power to give a helping hand to their country. Major Brooks, addressing the boys in St. ' George's Mission on Monday, said it was a very serious thing, and naturally many parents would he alarmed, but they could only be used for home defence. Undoubtedly some of them would have to make sacrifices, but before they had the parents consent forms filled up, they should ascertain from their employers if their jobs would be waiting for them when they got back. The Rev. J. M. Buckmaster impressed upon the boys that they should not have the parents' consent forms filled up if their duty was at home. They were not an organisation for fight- ing and killing—no Church organisation was for that purpose—but they believed in the end it would bring about peace. Further, they were only for defence. (Cheers.)

div.p: ST. PAUL'S COMPANY.

div.head: WARRINGTON WAR INCIDENTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON WAR INCIDENTS.
New Recruiting Depot. Cairo-street Schools were during this week opened as a recruiting depot for all branches of the service.
German Spy.
.-.- Rumour had it this week that a German spy had been examining a local bridge. No verifica- tion can be found for the story.
Ship Canal and Roads Guarded.
It is understood that the Ship Canal is now carefully guarded. Bridges and roads in the Warrington district are also wider guard.
Cheshire Lines Under Army Control.
_ The Cheshire Lines on Tuesday passed under the control of the Army Authorities. Hitherto it has been the main trunk lines linking up the North and South that have been so controlled.
Closed Station.
No one is now allowed on Bank Quay Station unless they have booked to some other place. Even the penny platform tickets are of no avail.
War Proclamations.
Some 18 proclamations relating to the war, received by the Town Clerk, are now on view in the public reading room.
Encamped in Bank Park. A number of the Army Service Corps have been encamped on the children's recreation ground in Bank Park.
Warrington's Aliens. All the aliens in Warrington are now believed to have registered at the Police Station, as re- quired by law. They do not number a hun- dred. .

div.p: Messrs._ Rylands. Very Busy.
- The works of Messrs. Rylands are now working at the highest possible pressure, and an extra night shift has had to be put on. Large quan- tities of barbed and ordinary wire are being made.

Prayers for a Speedy Peace. In the churche of all religious denominations in Warrington on Sunday prayers for a ispeedy termination of the war vPere offered. At the Wycliffe P.S.A. a similar prayer was delivered by the Chairman (Mr. B. Farrar).

div.head: Canal Tugs Commandeered.
div.p: Canal Tugs Commandeered.

Many of the hare tugs on the Bridgewater Canal, along with a large number of barges, have been commandeered for service, and in consequence the traffic on the Canal has de- creased to a marked extent.

div.head: Bravo, Church Lads!
div.p: Bravo, Church Lads!

_ Thirty-two members of the St. Paul's Com- pany Church Lads' Brigade—all over 17 years of age—have stated their willingness to join the Territorial Force. Already there are two officers and about twenty lads who are with the local Territorial Battalion.

div.head: Price of Commandeered Horses.
div.p: Price of Commandeered Horses.

Warrington horse owners, with rare excep- tions, have had some of their best horses com- mandeered. Messrs. Peter Walker and Son have lost a considerable number, as well as drays of different types. It is said that the price paid for the horses ranges from £25 to £35, accord- ing to age and quality.

div.head: Latest War "Catches."
div.p: Latest War "Catches."

"What's the war news?" queried a Warring- tonian of a local wag. " The Germans are in Berlin," came the answer. "Good gracious, never !" exclaimed the " surprised " questioner. "Ireland is surrounded," is another catch. The innocent naturally asked, "By the German fleet?" "By the sea" is the answer.

div.head: Warrington's_ German Prisoners.
div.p: Warrington's_ German Prisoners.

The German vessel Dyrade, captured over a week ago at the Walton lay-by, has since been taken by a British crew to Manchester, where other German prizes are in dock. The crew of seventeen are quartered at Warrington Police Station, where they spend their time playing cards and reading the English newspapers.

An Old Footballer's Adventure. At midnight on Wednesday a well-known old footballer saw two men acting suspiciously on the railway line near Latchford just as a train was due. He gave chase in his stockinged feet. One man got away, but the footballer captured the other, who denied that he was a German " spy," also stating that he was employed on the railway, and was looking for "spies."

div.p: Hippodrome Artiste .Arrested.

Owing to Mr. Flacori having been taken a prisoner of war "The Flacoris," lady and gentle- man. trapeze artistes, are unable to appear at the Hippodrome, where they were billenor this week. div.p: Grain Ship on the Canal.

Much interest was'taicen by Warringtonians on Sunday in the passage up the Ship Canal of the St. Helena. She left America with grain for Germany, but was diverted by the British Fleet and sent with her prize cargo to Manches- ter. The vessel is British, although the cargo was German.

A horse and carriage was being driven on the outskirts of Warrington on Thursday. when it was held up by two Army officials. The horse was taken out and run up and down before a veterinary inspector. div.p: Motor Cyclists and the War.
_ The Warrington motor cyclists have been ap- proached with the view of their giving the use of their machines for Army purposes. A splendid response is reported to have been made.

div.head: Infirmary and the War:
div.p: Infirmary and the War:

A special meeting- of the Board -of Manage- ment of the Warrington Infirmary is to be held on Friday to consider how far it is possible to place the resources of the Infirmary at the dis- posal of the Government.

Organising a Motor Service. Yesterday motor car owners in Warrington were asked by the Automobile Association if they would place their cars at the service of the country to operate within 100 miles of War- rington. A number wired that they would be pleased to do so.

div.head: Warrington Works Affected.
div.p: Warrington Works Affected.

ILast evening it was intimated that owing to the war the employes of Messrs. Fletcher, Rug- 'lsell and Co. would not work on Saturdays. The Iglass trade of Warrington is threatened with a shortage of material, although the question of short time has not yet been mentioned, the workers fear it may have to come.

div.head: Paper Money Galore.
div.p: Paper Money Galore.

When wages were paid in Warrington last night it was chiefly in the form of paper money, and the recipients were anxious to change-it as quickly as possible. In one hotel 150 pieces of " paper " were changed in a couple of hours. Other businesses felt the rush as keenly, and the stock of silver was nearly exhausted.

div.p: Soap Prices Unchanged.

div.head: "Spies," .at the _Swing Bridge.
div.p: "Spies," .at the _Swing Bridge.

The spy mania has evidently seized possession of the minds of worthy citizens, and this was illustrated by an incident which occurred at the Swing Bridge near Stockton Heath on Wednesday night. Two men were seen gazing at the Bridge by seven others. "German spies" were suspected, and the seven made after the two, who escaped in the darkness. The seven think they have done their country a service, but the other two were equally peaceful citizens.

div.head: Patriotic Foresters.
div.p: Patriotic Foresters.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Dis- trict Committee of the Ancient Order of Fores- ters WAR held at the Roebuck Hotel, Bridge- street, Bro. S. B. Healey, D.C.R., presiding. It was resolved that the district recommend the Courts to pay the contributions of those mem- bers who have been called to serve their King and country, and to keep them in benefit until their return. Also the district resolved to pay the contributions of the same members into the District Funeral Fund, and keep them in bene- fit for their funeral allowance in the district. The Courts in the district have agreed to comply with the recommendation. Not a Patriot.

An ex-soldier, who served in the Boer War, but has since tarnished his career, Patrick 31u1- larkey, of no fixed abode, was sentenced to three months' hard labour at Warrington Police Court on Thursday for the theft of three pairs of army boots from Orford Barracks. The Chief Constable said that accused had degener- ated into a sponger, and had come from Liver- pool to the Orford Barracks to sponge upon the good-heartedness of the reserves called up for service. Several witnesses spoke to seeing accused climbing over the barrack wall with army boots in his possession, and a sergeant of the South Lancashires said accused had repeat- edly been ordered out of the place.
A Deserting Patriot._

There was a decided element of romance at- tached to a case in which Joseph McGuire, a Warrington lad, was charged with being a deserter from the Royal Garrison Artillery sec- tion stationed at Port Royal, Jamaica. The Chief Constable said that McGuire got on board a. vefsel at Kingstown and worked his passage to Liverpool. When he deserted he had no idea that a war was brewing, but on reaching Liver- pool he learned that war had broken out. He offered to give himself up to the Liverpool police and at Seaforth Barracks, but they would not accept him, and he tramped to Warrington, where he gave himself up on Thursday morn- ing.—McGuire said he did not like Jamaica, so he left, but he wished to get hack to the army now war was on. He was remanded pending instructions from the War Office.

div.head: LOCAL PEOPLE IN GERMANY.
div.p: LOCAL PEOPLE IN GERMANY.
A Traveller Challenged.

A traveller connected with a well-known War- rington firm was challenged on Wednesday night by a Territorial stationed at Market Gate with being a German spy. A policeman was called, but the Warringtonian had sufficient evi- dence in his possession to show that he was a good Englishman. and he was allowed to go home in peace.

div.head: Post Office Recruits.
div.p: Post Office Recruits.

Owing to so many of the Warrington postal staff being called up for different phases of ser- vice in the Army, an auxiliary staff has had to be provided. This has been recruited from different classes of workers, including tanners who have been on strike, and engineers who have been temporarily unemployed. Additional telegraphic mes'sengers are also engaged to cope with the exceptionally heavy telegraphic busi- ness.

Not An Airship Light. As one of the last trams was crossing the War- rington Bridge the other evening a passenger Jumped up excitedly, exclaiming "The head- light of a German airship." Others scanned the . sky the direction indicated, and sure enough a bright light shone through a balloon-shaped thing. A little more examination showed that the light was a star shining through a small bank of cloud, and the passengers went home in a peaceful mind.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

'Street Traffic Regulations." Mr. George Chamberlain's letter under this -.heading' contained certain gratuitous impertin- ences which regular readers of this column will not expect me to notice particularly. As for his t direct que,tions to myself, only two seem to me to really molter; and on one of these I must ask for a little more light. Of course, the munici- pal authorities have "power to remove the time .limit on Corporation motor 'buses." They can regulate the running of their own vehicles within their own area. I am further asked: "Have the councillors power to impose a time limit?" This is altogether too vague for my, poor comprehension. Will the author be sufff- ciently explicit to make his meaning clear to a meaner intelligence? I will undertake to deal with it as soon as I am able to understand it or to perceive its drift. Meanwhile, let my humor- ous and logical friend be assured that I am no motorist's advocate, and that I by no Means think the attitude of the authorities in relation to offenders belonging to the class in question should be one of "masterly inactivity" or "benevolent neutrality." I trust he will favour me with a repetition in plain terms of what I suspect is intended for his most important question.

The Unspeakable Road Hog. Awaiting Mr. Chamberlain's good will and pleasure, I may just mention a recent experi- ence of my own while on a walking tour in East Lancashire. A simple-minded country gentle- man whose pretty garden adjoined the main road suffered much from the dust nuisance, and evidently thought to avoid this by a courteous 'appeal to scorchers. Projecting over his hedge was a board on which was painted the request: "Will motorists please drive slowly past this house?" On the other side were the words: "Thank you." Of course, going by on foot, I could read the inscriptions easily enough, but even as I did so, reckless criminals for whom they were intended were indulging in the utterly selfish pastime thus indicated :
