A Moot Point.

In a paragraph reproduoed in last week's "Table Talk" attention is called to the fact that men almost invariably wear out the sole of the left foot first, and one who essays to explain this attributes it " entirely " to the alleged habit of stepping off public vehidles in motion with that foot foremost! Now that will not do at all. I happen to have been long puzzled by the cir- cumstance as it affected myself, and it induced a pretty long course of personal observation at a period when and in districts where there were no trams and very few 'buses. I have noticed that most men stopping in the street for a chat rest more on the left than on 'the ri,glit foot, and that as they- turn to leave each Other they mostly wheel round upon the former. This strikes me as the more reasonable conclusion-of the matter.

Rough on His Lordship. An item in "Everywhere" showing the differ- ence between the sexes in their respective modes of treating certain things said to them reminded me of a sharp rebuke once administered by counsel to a judge who had the 'bad habit of needlessly interrupting legal argument. On the occasion referred to, with characteristic rude- ness, he said to an eminent member of the Bar who was addressing him at the moment, "What you are saying to me simply goes in at one ear and out at the other." "Just so, my lord," was the prompt retort, "What is there to pre- vent it?"

The Teacher Taught. True, that is a chestnut; but I have in reserve a brand new tit-hit—l had almost written that it was just forged and therefore fresh from the anvil, but that were to mix one's metaphors in- excusably, and I feel that at present I have enough laid to my charge without exposing my- self to more in the way of criticism. I have it from the teacher of a class in a church school that at a rKent examination in religious know- ledge the clerical inspector, entering the room in evident weariness toward the close of a heavy day, startled the drowsy youngsters by sud- denly demanding Who was Moses?" Receiv- ing no reply, he impatiently proceeded, "Come, now, who was Moses? Was he a man to begin with?" Then one little fellow recovered his power of speech, and treated the reverend inter- rogator to this gem, "No sir; p-please, sir, he was a baby to begin with."

div.head: "TUMULTUOUS WAR."
div.p: "TUMULTUOUS WAR."
Shakespearean Inspiration for the
Pres:nt Crisis.
IN THE NAME OF PEACE WE MOST "SWEAT TO PUT THE TYRANT DOWN."

Picking up my Shakespeare the other evening and casually glancing through its pages, ponder- ing meanwhile upon the events which have led up to the present European crisis, I was led to' peruse the volume to find what the bard of Strat- ford would. have said to us to-day had he been living in our age. I could not help but remem- ber that it was Goethe who said, "His plays are much more than poems," and that other writers had written of his inspired words as "those which helped tb,s-reader to realise the reality of his existence." Gne writer had said : " Shakespeare saw life stead!), and saw it whole," and as I continued to turn over the pages of my book, I recalled another phrase to the effect that "Amid experiences of life, often intensely bitter, ,Shakespeare had grown not only in mental stature, but learned moral sober- ness and spiritual wisdom."

TO BE RESISTED. Here was what I needed, for had not Mr. Asquith asked the nation to " keep cool," and the Peace Society called upon its members to maintain a calmness and exhibit a patience which are hard duties to perform in such a trying period? And so I resolved to see whether my favourite poet could help me, and wondering what his thoughts were upon war- fare, as to whether he favoured it or not, I found that he was very vehement against it. Using the lips of. the Bishop of Carlisle in "Richard II.," the poet gives vent to his feelings when war is suggested against the King in the words:—
"And in this seat of peace tumultuous wars Shall kin with kin and kind with kind con- found; Disorder, horror, fear and mutiny, Shall here inhabit and this land be call'd

The field of Golgotha and dead men's skulls. Or, if you raise this house against this house, It will the woefullest division prove That ever fell upon this cursed earth. Prevent, resist it, let it not be so, Lest child, child's children, cry against you woe 1"
This to me, as a member of the Peace Society, was very cheering; but had not events proved that war was practically inevitable, and, al- though bard to express the thought, perfectly justifiable?

div.head: WAR JUSTIFIED.
div.p: WAR JUSTIFIED.

Did Shakespeare ever find occasion to justify war, I wondered? Could I but find a sentence, which would help me in my theory that war was my country's only course to adopt? I was soon on the track, and remembering my read- ing in history of the battle of Bosworth Field, I found that Shakespeare justified the action of Richmond in his war upon Richard HI. in the words uttered by the future King : "Fellows in arms, and my most loving friends,
Bruie'd underneath the yoke of tyranny.
In God's fiame, cheerly on courageous friends, To reap the harvest of perpetual peace, By this one bloody trial of sharp war."

Is not peace the thing we seek? Would that it could be gained other than by war, I thought; but as it cannot be avoided. I sought to find what cheering wdid the poet could give me to maintain a calm and dignified patience. Not. far from Richmond's justification of his war, Shakespeare inspires me with the thought of a faith in the King of all kings, in the prayer uttered by Richmond as he knelt in his tent on the night preceding the battle:—

"0 Thou whose captain I account myself, Look on my forces with a gracious eye; Put in their hands Thy bruising ,irons of wrath, That they may crush down with a heavy fall The usurping helmets of our adversaries! Make us Thy ministers of chastisement, That we may praise Thee in Thy victory! To Thee I do commend my watchful soul Ere I let fall the windows of mine eyes : Sleeping and waking, 0, defend me still!"
"FREE YOUR CHILDREN FROM THE SWORD."

Here my thoughts wandered out to the field of action, and I turned over the pages to see what I could pass on to my comrades-in-arms as advice from the poet. Again, in "Richard Shakespeare remembers the troops, and puts his words into the mouth of Richmond as he says:—

" Then if you fight against God's enemy, God will, in justice, ,ward you as His soldiers; If you do sweat to put a tyrant down, You sleep in peace, the tyrant being slain; If you do fight against your country's foes, Your country's fat shall pay your pains the hire; If you do fight in safeguard of your wives, Your wives shall welcome home the con- querors; If you do free your children from the sword, Your children's children quit it in your age. Then in the name of God and all these rights, Advance your standards, draw your willing swords." Pursuing the cours9. of events, I paused to consider the action of many of my fellow- countrymen in their anxiety to secure for their own safe-keeping the hard-earned savings, which the banks had been allowed to guard up to the present time, and which, if unnecessarily withdrawn, would materially undermine the financial position of the country; or, again, what of the storing of food in the larders by those who, blessed by fortune's wheel, found themselves in a position to do it, thereby forc- ing up prices, and practically robbing the poor Of the necessaries of life? Selfishness, I thought.

ADVICE TO ALL Has Shakespeare no word for Me or others, if placed in similar situations, when in our hour of peril we need to stand shoulder to shoulder, bearing, if needs be, the burden of our weaker brethren? Presently my search was rewarded, for the poet gives to us a golden rule to govern our principles, nay, not only for the present, but for all time, in the ethic* given by Polonius, in "Hamlet," to Laertes:— " This above all,—To thine own self be true, And it must follow 1s the night the day Thou canst not then be false to any man."

Over and over again my eyes are drawn ts pregnant sentences which hold in themselves much that is applicable to us at the present time, but two thoughts suggested themselves to me: (1) as to what Shakespeare would say of what we know as " mafficking." Listen as Hamlet gives advice : " In the very torrent, tempest, and, as I must say, the whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that may give it smoothness." And (2) as to whether he held with the over- indulgence of intoxicating liquors during otfr seasons of rejoicings, when news .of victories reach us from time to time. I find that the poet held an opinion which voiced itself over and over again in the words of many of his characters, to the effect that he felt the shame of drunkenness as a national vice. It was Cassio who, in "Othello," wailed to lago, after a night of revelling, that he had lost the "immortal part of himself and thal which remains is bestial," and as I read the words I earnestly expressed the hope that in the midst of our country's triumphs my fellow-country- men would be kept from "losing the immortal part" of themselves through_ over-indulgence in the "cup" which is supposed "to cheer." Before concluding my perusal of the book • . , 7{Continue 4 int next. Column.)

THE PASSING .OF THE YEARS. 'Mid the heather on the hillside, Up in Scotland far away, There's a cosy little cottage, And its stones are old and gray; / But 'tis there I spent my childhood, And my eyes grow dim with tears, As the fleeting vision Tadeth With the passing of the years.

When the sun was slowly setting, And the birds retired to rest, I would sit upon the door-stone, Gazing out towards the west; Whilst my father smoked his " warden " In the tranquil evening air, And my mother read the Bible Or sent up a silent prayer.

It is good to thank the Giver, When the toil of day is done, For the peaceful, .happy moments, At the setting of the sun; And the lessons learnt in childhood Make us proof against the fears Which would hold the soul in torment With the passing of the years. '

Now My duties as a soldier Find me in the desert hare, With grim warriors all aro and me, Who my every danger share. Yet amidst the stress of conflict Comes the cry which ever cheers; I will guard thee now and ever, In the passing of the years.

TOLSTOI'S. LESSON. Objection to violence and cruelty, which was so characteristic of Tolstoi, began, according to a recent biography, in early childhood. In a short story he wrote for the use of school chil- dren he tells how he once used to ride the old horse, Raven, after his brothers had each had a turn on it; and how, since Raven was too tired to move from the stable, he beat it till he broke his switch on its sides. He then demanded a stouter switch from the serf in charge, but the man replied Ali, master, have you no pity! Why do you beat him? He is twenty years old and is tired Out; he can hardly breathe. Why, for a horse, he is as old as Timofeyitch "—a very old peasant living on the place. "You might as well get on Timofeyitch's back and drive him beyond his strength like that, with a switch. Would you feel no pity for him?"

_ I thought of Timofeyitch and harkened to the man. I got off the horse's back, and when I noticed how its streaming sides were working, and how heavily it breathed through its nos- trils, swishing its thin tail, I understood how hard it was for it. Till then I had thought it was as happy as was myself. And I felt so sorry for Raven that I began to kiss his sweaty neck and to beg his pardon for having beaten him.
Since then I have grown up, but I always have pity on horses, and always remember Raven and Timofeyitch when I see horses ill-treated.

FORTUNES MADE FROM PLAYS: To-day a successful novelist looks, 'frequently with splendid realisation, to profits to be made on the stage after his or her) story has run through the circulating libraries. Anstey Guthrie told me that the proceeds of the serial and book publication of "The Man from Blank- nor s." handsome as they were, were trifles compared with the aggregate of the royalties yielded by the comedy. The presentation in dramatic form of" The Bondman" brought its author pecuniary benefit far exceeding the,pro- ceeds of (he copyright of his novel. The almost fabulous amount of profit on a successful play was revealed in connection with the production. of " Charley's Aunt." When Penley proposed to run the piece, all he wanted was money to meet expenses. By chance he met a lady who knew a man with money at his command and disposition to venture it on theatrical enterprise. Penley, having noth- ing, and therefore ready to 'promise anything, undertook to pay the lady five per cent, on his profits if she would obtain for him a loan of ~tBOO. She, going to work with that appear- ance of artlessness which is among the charms of woman, induced her friend to plank down the money. Incidentally she secured from the lender a promise also to pay a percentage on profits that might come to him from the trans- action. Under these arrangements she seemed pretty well off. So she was. But her share of the earnings of " Charley's 'Aunt" was a mere trifle compared with the revenue that flowed into the coffers of lender and borrower. From the two principals the lady who had been at the trouble of personally introducing them drew commission amounting to £1,700. The investor of £BOO received dividends amounting to £30,000, whilst Fenley pocketed £6o,ooo.—From the August "Strand Magazine."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. A Genuine Lancashire Play.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. A Genuine Lancashire Play.

In Lancashire "The Pride o' the Mill" is sure to meet with success, and patrons of the Royal Court Theatre have been more than (he- lighted with Mr. Harry FoxwelPs production this week, for there is a good sound plot, and despite the fact that it is on somewhat usual -lines, the manner in which every incident is brought out in homely dialect makes it quite acceptable. A young wayward girl, tired of hum-drum home life, made terribly hard by a stringent step-mother, lends her ear to the plausible tongue of an unscrupulous adventurer and an equally heartless adventuress, whose combined efforts result in the girl leaving her home for gaiety and "life" in the "world." Just at the point when the schemers are rub- bing their hands at the success of their mach- inations the girl stolidly refuses to let herself be sold into bondage to a callous foreigner. After many exciting scenes, in which a duel with knives figures prominently, the girl is rescued by her Lancashire lover, whom she afterwards marries and happiness is once more paramount in the Lancashire cottage by the mill. The company is an exceptionally clever one, the authoress (Miss Sheila Walsh) playing the part of Jessie Butterworth with much feel- ing. The emotions are stirred by the powerful acting of Mr. Henry Scathard as the father of the girl, whose love for his daughter leads him near to distraction. Miss Baby Hughes is a " proverbial " cat-like step-mother, and Mr. Holland Day scores a success as the stolid Lancashire lover. Mr. Herbert Fare makes the part of the adventurer as repulsive as pos- sible, and Miss Ruth Zillwood makes him an able partner. Mr. Harrison Ford also earns the execrations of the "popular" parts as Don Bruno Di Vilanos. The comedy element is ably maintained by Mr. W. H. Irving and Miss Ciisie Cleveland as Mr. and Mrs. Percy GeOrge Shuttleworth, who also aid in the 'unmasking of the schemers.

The Back Fastening. At the beginning of this year the welcome news that dresses and blouses were to be fas- tened in front went forth; now hack fastenings are seen again on many of the newest models for Autumn wear. These consist of a close row of buttons and buttonholes, that trim the back. However, as individuality is permitted in the choice of styles, it is possible that both fashions will prevail, and that women will please themselves in this matter. Front fas- tenings are so much more sensible and con- venient than those at the ,back, and it seems foolish to revive the latter. A model somewhat in the Princess style, with panniers and cape, %fastened( with buttons at the back, and one in Russian blouse style had halftone from. the back of ther neck to the edge of the tunic. Another revival to be noted in early autumn modes is the return of the redingote. Its prin. cipal characteristics are its long, straight lines, and absence of waist line. The Mantelette. _ _

No garment could be easier to fashion at home than the little mantelette, that is one of the most popular shoulder wraps. of the moment. It requires no lining, and can be made without a pattern from an odd length of silk picked up during the sales. It is merely a long scarf draped on the shoulders by being caught together to -make sleeves, just at the waist. Lace finishes the V-shaped opening, which is quite low in front. A sash of some soft silk, half the width being sufficient, makes a smart finish, especially if fastened at the side and one end is allowed to fall to below the cape. Quite small remnants can be used to make dainty blouses of the kimono order, if care is exercised in choosing these short lengths. If the blouses so made were bought in a shop they would cost treble the price of the rem- nants and be no better, if as good, in quality.

Collars and Gloves. Collars just now 'strike a rather uncertain note. Designers have had recourse to portraits of Oliver Cromwell and pictures of .Romney, Raeburn, as well as to those of the Medici, and, Marie Stuart, and as a natural result there is much diversity in shapes. Many of the newest collars in fine lace or lawn have tiny specks of

colour, or gold, worked on them in delicate silks. Touches of colour are seen also on the backs of gloves, whether short or long'; generally these match the dresses, when made of coloured materials, or they afford a contrast to white gowns of lace or muslins. Vandyke points in a contrasting shade of kid are used in a novel way to ornament the long gloves worn chiefly by debutantes. The edging goes from the top of the glove towards the wrist. Woolwork is seen' again as revers and cuffs for suits of serge, covert coating, &c., in fine cross-stitch, mostly in shades of red. Leather is also used in this connection. Wide and narrow silk braids trim tailored suits, and more especially the new cape-coats of covert coating, tweed or homespun.

Fashionable Footgear. The vogue for black and white has affected the season's footgear, and white kid and black suede are combined very often in walking shoes. White uppers are seen too with patent leather fronts and sidee, and white buckskin, with black heels, looks very well. Stone or putty shades, and black are also shown in the newest shoes. A pretty idea for evening wear comes from America. Instead of buckles, beautiful floral decorations, consisting of artificial flowers, are used on the front of the shoe. White also has had an astonishing vogue this year, and white shoes and stockings• were never more popular. Yet they suit only the woman or girl blessed with slim ankles and narrow feet. A big foot is at its best in black hose and shoes, and these can be worn with white• dresses, and look ex- ceedingly well if a note of black appears on the dress.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Danger from Gnats and Mosquitos.

Attention has once more been drawn to the danger arising from the bites of mosquitos and gnats by the death of Chief Inspector Roiph from a gnat bite. Chief Inspector Rolph, who was•4s years of age and a man of great physical strength, was in charge of the police arrange- ments at Bisley. On Friday he was bitten by a gnat, and within a few hours signs of blood. poisoning appeared. He was taken to the hos- pital, where he died about 48 hours later. . It is not generally recognised in England how serious bites of this kind may prove. The culicidce—the blood-sucking branch of the diptera—which include the various species of mosquitos and gnats, are well-known as carriers of disease, especially in hotter countries, and malaria, yellow fever, filariasis, and a number of other diseases are known to be widely dissem- inated by the mosquito. But it is not only in the Tropics that they are dangerous. Even within the Arctic circle they are abundant in many localities, and exceedingly, bloodthirsty during the short summer. In England and countries with a similar climate they are also abundant, but they are only troublesome during hot weather, when their thirst for blood is stimulated by the heat. During the recent heat wave, they have become so plentiful, espe- cially in the South of England, that they have almost amounted to a plague, and many cases have been reported of more or less serious bites. In England, of course, there is no danger of infection froin. the diseases disseminated by tropical mosquitos, but the gnat bite often leads to blood-poisoning. There was a case last week in which a man lost the sight of his eye through the bite of a gnat. The preliminary stages of all mosquitos are passed in water, either fresh or salt, stagnant or slightly mov- ing, and while the larvie of some species are found in natural pools and ditches, many mos- quitos infest houses and breed even in the slightest accidental accumulation of water, such as may have collected in a discarded bottle nr tin.—" The Times."

div.head: PUBLIC PARKS OF BELFAST.
div.p: PUBLIC PARKS OF BELFAST.

At the present time Belfast is the centre of world-wide interest, and it may therefore be in- teresting to give an account of her parks .and gardens, and thus show that her works of peace are not eclipsed by her preparations for war. Belfast is in many respects an up-to-date city. It is noted for its large industries (seven of Which are the largest in the world), and stran- gers to the city are much struck by its fine buildings, among which might be mentioned the magnificent City Hall, which' stands in its own well laid out grounds, and the Municipal Technical Institute, which caters for 7,000 stu- dents.

The parks of Belfast are of recent develop- ment. Prior to 1869 there were none under pub- lic control, yet despite this fact there are no less than seven parks, with a total area of about 400 iicres, under the charge of the Parks and Ceme- teries Committee of the County Borough Council of Belfast.—" Agricultural Economist and Horti- cultural Review."

div.head: Gem of the Month.
div.p: The Gem of the Month.

The ruby is dedicated to the month of August, and is believed by the superstitious to bring luck to lovers. It is accounted a sacred stone in Burma, and is supposed to have been ono of the five gems that composed the wonderful necklace of Vishnu, the Hindoo goddess. The Burmese believe that the ruby has, like fruit, its various stages of existence. At first it is without colour, then it becomes yellow, green and blue, and finally, when quite ripe, a deep red. The crystal is also believed to bring good luck by the superstitious, possibly because it is used by for- tune-tellers and soothsayers. Cut as a prism it is now worn as a pendant suspended on a slender gold or silver chain.

Mulberry Wine. The mulberries must be quite ripe—gathered on a dry day. Look them over, bruise them with a wooden spoon in a tub, putting a quart of water to each quart of fruit, and the juice and thinly-cut rind of two lemons to each quart. Add to each gallon 41b. of moist sugar; mash and stir this until it ferments. Then either bottle it or put it into a clean cask, straining it through a clean coarse cloth. Let the bottles or the cask stand for a day before storing the wine. Sweeping._

. - In the first place, everything that can be re- moved from the room in the way of furniture and ornaments should first be carefully brushed and dusted, and then taken into the hall or into another room. The remainder of the furniture should be covered, and if the curtains are not taken down they should be pinned up short, or the ends put into linen bags. Salt brightens and cleans a carpet beautifully, but it absorbs moisture and rusts the tacks. As long as there is any salt left in the carpet, and it is extremely difficult to sweep it all up, just as long will there be moisture collecting. Always sweep in one direction with a short, hard stroke. CoVer the broom with a flannel cloth, and wipe the walls with a downward stroke. Sweep out the corners. div.head: FEDERAL SOLUTION.
div.p: THE FEDERAL SOLUTION.

History and precedents teach us that we may have a Union which is Federal between widely divergent classes of people divergent in num- bers, as in New York and Oregan, Ontario—and Prince Edward Island, New South Wales and West Australia, Prussia and Bavaria; divergent in race as in Ontario and Quebec; and divergent in geographical extent, as over the Continents of Canada, Germany, United States, Australia and South Africa, or over the insignificant terri- tory of Switzerland. The Federal Union is the one and only political Union that can reconcile divergent races, views and interests, and remain stable, smooth, progressive and indissoluble, under all circumstances. Even the widely divergent views, Ideals and interests held rela- tively by the North at'a the South in the United States half a century ago, were not inconsistent with stable political Union; nor could that Union be dissolved even by all the force of one of the Most determined and bloody civil wars in history. Home Rule, then, is inevitable. Exclusion at the present time is impossible; and we are left to find Ulster a home in a local Parliament or give her a Parliament of her own.—Dr. Chapple, M.P., in the August "Contemporary Review."

div.head: FATAL KINDNESS.
div.p: A FATAL KINDNESS.
Youth who went for "Pea Blowers ''
Drowned.

There was .a sequel to the drowning fatality in the River Mersey at the Warrington Coroner's Court on Monday, when Mr. S. Brighouse con- ducted an inquest on James Stanley. Tbmlinson 18), 4, Old-road.

William Tomlinson, labourer, said the de- ceased, who was his son, had been subject to epileptic fits for the past three years, and as a conseqnence he had not followed any regular employment. On the previous Thursday his son brought witness his dinner to Walton, and then appeared to be in his usual health, which was good when, he was not troubled with fits. After receiving his dinner witness received the assur- ance from his son that he would go straight home. The youth went down Chester-road, and at 6.13 p.m., when witness arrived home he dis- covered that his son had not returned. He re- ported the matter to the police, and was in- formed fhat a youth had fallen into the river near Chester-romkearlier in the day. He got assistance and commenced dragging the river, and recovered the body. In answer to the Coroner, witness said that the body was about six or eight feet from the side of the river.' A boy named Samuel Day, 158, Knutsford- road, said that at 12.10 p.m. on Thursday he was with two other boys in Chester-road, and saw Tomlinson on the inside of the railings which ran alongside the river. In reply to a question from Tomlinson, he and his companion said they would like a "pea blower" (which grew by the river side), and he gave them one each. Deceased then said, "Watch me get some more," and went down to the water's edge, where he com- menced to cut some more "pea blowers." All at once he turned round and commenced to sing and dance, and then fell backwards into the water. He 'appeared to try to pull off his jacket, and, after struggling, sank. He came up again. and then sank for the last time. Witness added that he told some men on bicycles what had hap- pened, but they took no notice. He and:his com- panion went to the Police Station and reported the matter.
The Coroner : No doubt when he was singing and dancing the youth had had another seizure. "Accidentally drowned" was the jury's ver- dict.

div.head: MORE HOPEFUL POSITION.
div.p: A MORE HOPEFUL POSITION.
"EXAMINER" SPECIAL

The art of keeping cool, as recommended by Mr. Asquith, during the present national crisis, is now in practice in Warrington, as elsewhere, and the result is found reflected in the, approxi- mately, normal price which now prevails for food-stuffs. "The Examiner" representative is assured by many of the Warrington shop- keepers that if the public continue to " kz.AT cool" there need be no fear of a food famine.

"Stock-taking in the great warehouses," said one, " has been in progress during last week-end, and the result has proved eminently satisfactory. It has been discovered that there is a larger quantity- of food stored in this coun- try than was generally supposed. The latest computation shows that of the common ne.:es- sities of life—luxuries are excluded—we have within our tight little island enough to keep us going for five months, and every day sees the arrival of fresh supplies. For instance, two large grain ships have passed up the Ship Canal in two days. Liverpool, Glasgow, Hull, Leith and other ports announce fresh arrivals of the material which constitutes 'the staff of life.' I hardly think there will be any marked increase in the price of the common necessities of life—truly reassuring news."

div.p: PRICES IN THREE GREAT WARS.

It is interesting to compare the prices in the last two great wars with those of the present, and the comparison proves that we are in a much better position in 1914 than were our fore- fathers of 1870 or 1854, the last two being the dates upon which the Franco-Prussian and the Crimean Wars broke out. div.head: PEACE SOCIETY PROPOSAL.
div.p: PEACE SOCIETY PROPOSAL.

The following appeal has been issued by the Peace Society, August sth, 1914 Now that war has been declared, and the last hope of maintaining the neutrality of this coun- try has been cut off, the Peace Society, which for nearly a century has represented the cause of International Peace, appeals to the people of this country.
The views of this Society in respect to war are well known, and they are in no way affected by this fresh outbreak, but if they had been fol- lowed there would have been no war.

War, it insists, is a crime, and between Chris- tian peoples it should be unthinkable. It is especially to be noted, that preparation for war necessarily leads to war, and that large armies and navies are always a menace to Peace.

But war is in progress, and the practical ques- tion now is, What should be done? It is too late to talk of neutrality or of mere details. The Soeieby appeals to the people to maintain a dig- nified and patient self-control, to restrain all ebullitions of feeling and passion, and to avoid all harsh and irritating speech towards those who are in conflict. It appeals to all to hold themselves in check, and, while praying for the return of Peace. to be on the alert for every opening that may lead towards it.

Colonel Chaloner asked whether the repre- sentative of the War Office was aware that Army officers Were commandeering all horses in places where the harvest had only just begun; whether in the interests of the food supply of the country he could prevent this in the future, and whether the horses already taken could be restored to their owners until the harvest had been gathered in. He had received a telegram saying that in one district all the horses had been taken.

Mr. Tennant said that this question was ex- ercising the War Office very considerably and that it distressed him to hear of the cases to which the hon. member had drawn attention. Every possible facility would be given to farmers and those engaged in breeding stock. He had had an interview on Friday with a gdntleman who was in a state of much anxiety as half the number of his horses had been commandeered. He had communicated with the Remoutit Depart- ment asking them to reduce the number of horses taken in this case. The reply was that, of course, they would do so, if desired, but that they might have to come back and say that the number of horses they had wassinsufficient. He appealed to all those interested in horses to co-operate as far as pessible with the Remount Department, in order that the requirements of the Army might be served. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Runciman : May I supplement whit has been said? The Board of Trade has had the very willing co-operation from firms and busi- ness men whose requirements with regard to motor lorries and horses were not so pressing, and they have shown a public spirit with re- gard to the distribution Of food, which, I hope, will be copied by all other owners of horses and motor vehicles.

div.head: SPECIALLY COMPILED FOR "THE EXAMINER.'
div.p: SPECIALLY COMPILED FOR "THE EXAMINER.'
SECOND

The news that appears in the daily newspapers, most of it of the sensational kind and largely based on rumours without foundation, is con- fusing to the ordinary reader. We shall from week to week provide our readers with a straightforward summary of events, from which will be eliminated all news that is not officially confirmed or properly authenticated. They will thus be provided with a bird's-eye view of all that has really taken place.
EEK. GERMANS SHORT OF FOOD.
Several individuals from German patrols have been captured both in France and Bel_ g ium. In all cases they are reported to be short of food for both men and horses and to have made no resistance.

div.head: EARLY MOVEMENTS.
div.p: EARLY MOVEMENTS.
Up to Tuesday, when the official news bureau was opened, the whereabouts of the British and French Armies was being kept a profound secret.

At this period of hostilities no news of any importance can be expected, was the official report. Any movements of the British Army or of those of the nations with which it is co- operating can naturally not be divulged, and over the proceedings of the enemy lies the fog of war. There is good reason to believe that the mass of the German troops on the Western frontier are distributed between Thionville and Liege. This was taken to mean that Germany was concentrating her troops in South-eastern Bel- gium, and Luxemburg, her main attack upon France being designed to take place along a line from Thionville to Liege, about 150 miles apart..

With six Army Corps held back by Germany to defend the Russian frontier, the German force actually in line of battle has been esti- mated to total, approximately, 1,000,000 men. To these France and her Allies can oppose more men, more sabres, more and better guns.

div.head: IN BELGIUM. THE GERMAN ATTACK DEVELOPS.
div.p: IN BELGIUM. THE GERMAN ATTACK DEVELOPS.

At noon on Tuesday it was officially reported that about two German Cavalry divisions were in the neighbourhood of Tongres ; three German corps were still opposite Liege; other German troops were reported to be entrenching the line of the River Aisne. • .
The large German Force was moving through Luxemburg, and the advanced troops were on the Belgian frontier.

THE GALLANT DEFENCE OF LIEGE. It was stated that the Germans had lost about 8,000 killed before Liege. An unconfirmed report, published on Tues- day, stated that the principal Liege forts were still holding out, though some of the smaller forts had been captured. The bombardment of the forts was proceeding without intermission. On one occasion a fort was apparently silenced, but when the German infantry advanced to the attack a hail of bullets was poured into them so suddenly and so effectively that they retired with heavy loss. The attackers, whd were constantly being reinforced, displayed great courage. It is stated that 120,000 are engaged in the attack. Refugees from Liege describe the conditions as terrible. Many houses in the town of Liege have been damaged or burnt.

div.head: MAIN GERMAN FORCE SOUTH OF THE
div.p: MAIN GERMAN FORCE SOUTH OF THE
MEUSE.

The Official Press Bureau issued the follow- ing at 3.30 a.m. on Thursday An engagement has been in progress north- west of Hasselt between a Belgian Cavalry division supported by a brigade of Infantry and what is supposed to be the 'second German Cavalry division, 2,500 strong, supported by a battalion of Infantry and twelve guns. The fourth German Cavalry division is re- ported to be moving to Jodoine. No German Infantry is known of on the left bank of the Meuse except the above battalion. The Germans are entrenching at Vise. The Liege forts are holding out. The Ger- mans are 4onstructing batteries on the north of Liege preparatory to a siege. Heavy guns have already been heard. The Germans are constructing a railway between Vise and Hom- burg parallel to the frontier of Dutch Limburg and are entrenching themselves in Liege itself. Huy, Marche, and Houffalise form points on the west border region held by the German Cavalry. Columns of German Cavalry are moving towards the Ourthe.

div.head: ALSACELORRAINE.
div.p: ALSACE- LORRAINE.
AGGRESSIVE FRENCH RE-ENTER TIIEIR OLD TERRITORY.

Last week-end France and the world was electrified by the news that a French force had entered Alsace, defeated a German force there, and occupied Mulhausen, twenty miles over the frontier. They afterwards retired from the town to a neighbouring entrenched position. Exaggerated accounts of this achievement were published and huge losses were spoken of. The affair appears to have been merely a reconnaissance in force in accordance with a pre- determined plan of campaign. It has had a great moral effect, the successes of the French troops having been received with acclamation by the people of Alsace and of France.

The value of the movement lay in the fact that it proved that the French were prepared to take the initiative and that they again had their feet in Alsace "after 44 years of sorrowful waiting," as the French Commander-in-Chief put it.

The News Bureau on Thursday reported that the French retreat from Mulhausen was well carried out. The opposing forces were in the proportion of four Germans to one French. The German Field Artillery proved inferior to the French, and the bursts of shrapnel were indif- ferent. The German Heavy Artillery was not as effective as was expected.

On the Russo-Austrian frontier Cavalry en- counters took place early this week, and an Austro-Hungarian advance towards Kielce was reported.
THE NORTH SEA.
SUBMARINE ATTACK ON BRITISH
CRUISERS. GERMAN BOAT SUNK.

The Secretary of the Admiralty in a com- munication on Sunday night stated "One of the cruiser squadrons of the main fleet was attacked yesterday by German sub- marine. None of His Majesty's ships were damaged, and one of the enemy's submarines- 15—was sunk." It was officially announced that the Birming- ham, a light/cruiser, was responsible for this feat. Beyond this nothing is known.
IN THE MEDITER- RANEAN. THE FUGITIVE GERMAN WAR- SHIPS' INGLORIOUS FATE.

There are very good reasons for believing that the German warships Goeben and Breslau have taken refuge in the Dardanelles, and that both ships will be dealt with according to interna- tional usage. With the dismantlement and internment of these .ships the safety of trade will be almost entirely secured. Since the above report was issued it has been ascertained that these German vessels have been purchased by Turkey to repair the loss which she has suffered through the action of Great Britain i,o tcking over the two warships which were building for her in this country. Both ships date from 1911. The Goeben, one of the finest ships in the German Navy, cost about £1,250,000, and the Breslau about .4391,480. The Goeben in particular was specially designed by Professor Kretsschner to challenge the British Dreadnought supremacy.

div.head: IR, SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1914.
div.p: IR, SATURDAY, AUGUST 15, 1914.
GERMAN COLONI SEIZED.
BRITISH AND FRENCH ENTRY INTO TOGOLAND.
The Admiralty have issued the following official statement :

"Acting on instructions from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, the British forces in the Gold Coast Colony yesterday seized the Port of Lome in German Togoland on the West Coast of Africa. No resistance was offered, and South Togoland up to 120 kilometres north from the coast was simultaneously surrendered." The French Embassy has received informa- tion from Paris that a British force has seized , the port of Lome, in Togoland, and that French troops have entered the colony by way of I Dahomey. Togoland, which is situated on the Gulf of Guinea, forms part of the territory formerly distinguished as the Slave Coast. It was an- nexed by Germany in 1884. It has an area of 33.659 square miles and a coloured population of about 1,000,000. Last year the European resi- dents numbered 368, of whom 320 were Germans: Togoland was ruled by an Imperial Governor, Duke Adolphus Frederick of Mecklenburg, assisted by a council of seven unofficial mem- bers. Lome is the capital of the colony.

div.head: SAFETY OF THE
div.p: SAFETY OF THE
SEAS.
THE NAVY ABLE TO PROTECT COMMERCE.

The Admiralty publicly express their fun con- fidence in the Navy's ability to protect the trade routes between Britain and South America and across the Atlantic generally. Twenty-four British cruisers, with help from French vessels, are searching for the five German cruisers known to be in that ocean and now hunted too con- tinually and kept too busy to do mischief. In the North Sea there is less certainty of safety for merchant shipping. The Germans are known to have scattered mines indiscrimin- ately, and this is, of course, the theatre where naval hostilities may take place at any moment.

div.head: SITUATION LAST NIGHT.
div.p: SITUATION LAST NIGHT.
CONTINUED SUCCESSES OF THE
ALLIES.

The following communique was issued by the official Press Bureau yesterday afternoon:— After successful resistance for five days at the passes of St. Marie Aux Mines and Le /fon- homme, the French troops have "oi7(TupTed the region of the Saale Pass, which commands the valley of the Bruche, an affluent of the Rhine. It is now confirmed that in Belgium the Bel- gians were successful in an engagement which took place on August 12 between ileir troops and six regiments of German cavalfy, sup- ported by 2,500 infantry, machine guns, and artillery. The enemy -was completely disor- ganised, the six cavalry regiments suffering the losses, and the Belgians pursued the infantry, which gave way this (Friday) morning towards Eghezee, sixteen kilos to the north of Namur. A mixed detachment from the garrison sur- prised some German cavalry regiments in camp, threw them into confusion, and forced them back towards the east after tating numerous prisoners and capturing cannon and machine guns, . . .

--- Liege forts are reported to he still holding out and to have plenty of supplies. Belgian cyclists and cavalry from Namur sur- prised yesterday a force of German cavalry, accompanied by artillery and machine guns, and compelled them to retire. The Germans lost a field gun and several machine guns.

THE RIGHT TO A LIVING WAGE. We come back to the "Living Wage" as the condition of securing a living soul, a personality alive on all its sides, and in possession of all its native powers. This is the true end of all human efforts both individual and social, that by which civilisation itself must in the last .resort be tested. Justice demands thal the rights of property shall bend to the superior rights of men to a living wage—including, of course, the employer's own bona-fide needs as a man. In this sense the living wage for all the workers must be the first moral charge on profits. It is for employers, as good citizens, as humanitarians, as Christians in particular, to prove whether they realise the meaning of their own profession, and will obey it.—Dr. Vernon Bartlet in the August "Contemporary Review."
